title: Reimagining the Legal Industry: Insights from the Pathways Project
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI requires redesign of legal-service delivery rather than simple tool adoption, and materially extends it with a strategic transition framework: outcomes-based value, scalable platforms, dynamic data and trusted multidisciplinary expertise. Its contribution is forward-looking and workshop-based, however, rather than evidence that Harvey or another vertical vendor will become durable infrastructure.
qs: Using the Three Horizons Framework to shape the workshop, the report identifies six key shifts shaping this transition, including movement from billable hours to outcomes-based value, from bespoke work to scalable platforms, and from static documents to dynamic data models.

Pathways underscores that firms remain central to shaping what comes next, identifying how leading firms can move from labor-intensive production toward platforms of trusted, multidisciplinary expertise that deliver speed and confidence at scale.

kp.k: Pathways explores legal industry evolution through 2040
kp.d: In this January 5, 2026 article, Harvey reports the first-phase findings of the Pathways Project, released by The LegalTech Fund and developed with Harvey. The project convened industry leaders, with Leaders’ Quest supporting facilitation and program design and ALM acting as data and media partner. Its account is a forward-looking strategic exercise about AI and technology through 2040; the article provides no participant count or quantitative study results.
qs: Pathways convened a group of industry leaders, with Leaders’ Quest supporting facilitation and program design and ALM serving as the data and media partner, to examine how the legal industry may evolve through 2040 under the impact of AI and technology.
The report is intended as a strategic guide for law firm leaders navigating AI transformation, hybrid talent models, and changing legal economics.

kp.k: AI pressures traditional leverage and raises client expectations
kp.d: Harvey characterizes the Pathways findings as indicating an industry inflection point: continued strong firm performance coexists with AI- and data-driven changes in work and value creation. The reported pressures concern traditional leverage models and clients’ demands for transparent, predictable services and commercially relevant advice. No specific staffing ratios or measured changes in client expectations are supplied.
qs: The Pathways findings indicate that the legal industry is at a true inflection point.

While firms continue to perform well, AI and data are reshaping how work is done and how value is created, placing pressure on traditional leverage models and elevating client expectations around transparency, predictability, and advice tied directly to business priorities.

kp.k: Pricing, production and information models are expected to shift
kp.d: The article reports that the workshop used the Three Horizons Framework to identify six transition shifts, naming three: billable hours toward outcomes-based value, bespoke work toward scalable platforms, and static documents toward dynamic data models. These are presented as a framework for understanding market evolution, rather than quantified adoption findings; the remaining three shifts are not specified in this article.
qs: Using the Three Horizons Framework to shape the workshop, the report identifies six key shifts shaping this transition, including movement from billable hours to outcomes-based value, from bespoke work to scalable platforms, and from static documents to dynamic data models.
Together, these shifts provide a framework for understanding how the legal market is evolving.

kp.k: Firms can build scalable platforms of multidisciplinary expertise
kp.d: Harvey reports Pathways’ strategic argument that firms retain a central role during a transition in which new scalability models coexist with established approaches. The opportunity described is to invest and adapt away from labor-intensive production toward trusted multidisciplinary expertise delivered through platforms, with speed and confidence at scale. This is framed as a possible direction for leading firms, not an accomplished industry-wide transformation.
qs: As the industry enters a transition period in which new forms of scalability are emerging alongside established approaches, firms face choices about where to invest and how to adapt.

Pathways underscores that firms remain central to shaping what comes next, identifying how leading firms can move from labor-intensive production toward platforms of trusted, multidisciplinary expertise that deliver speed and confidence at scale.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team, summarising the Pathways findings, claims that AI and data are changing legal production and value creation, pressuring traditional staffing leverage and raising client expectations.
pts.d: The article describes an industry inflection point despite continued strong firm performance. It reports shifts toward outcomes-based value rather than billable hours, scalable platforms rather than bespoke work, and dynamic data models rather than static documents. It also presents a prospective path for leading firms: moving from labour-intensive production to scalable platforms of trusted, multidisciplinary expertise. These are reported industry trends and strategic possibilities, not quantified outcomes or inevitable predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated basis is the Pathways Project’s first-phase findings, derived from an industry-leader workshop organised around the Three Horizons Framework.
pts.d: The Harvey Team attributes the findings to Pathways, developed by The LegalTech Fund in partnership with Harvey. Leaders’ Quest supported facilitation and programme design, and ALM was the data and media partner. The supplied article offers workshop-based strategic synthesis and industry authority; it does not present numerical data, benchmark results, named firm case studies, or measured effects supporting the claims. ALM’s role does not itself establish that any particular empirical result is reported here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes a transition already underway as of January 5, 2026, within a scenario-planning horizon extending through 2040.
pts.d: The 2040 horizon concerns how the industry may evolve, not a firm deadline for each shift. Existing approaches and new forms of scalability are expected to coexist during the transition. The proposed move toward multidisciplinary platforms is framed as something leading firms can pursue through investment and adaptation, rather than as an assured outcome for all firms. No dates or adoption rates are given for individual changes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms and their leaders, with clients shaping expectations for service delivery and value.
pts.d: Firm leaders face investment and adaptation choices involving AI transformation, hybrid talent models, staffing leverage, and changing economics. Leading firms are identified as potential providers of scalable, multidisciplinary expertise. Clients are described as expecting greater transparency, predictability, and advice aligned with business priorities. The article does not quantify employment effects or distinguish impacts by firm size, lawyer seniority, or client segment.
